newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cuts Argentina trade benefits in patent dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cuts Argentina trade benefits in patent dispute.

text.p: President Clinton on Tuesday ordered a cut in the number of Argentine goods that can be imported duty free to protest what he said was a failure to protect patents and other intellecutal property.

An order signed by Clinton, reduces by 50 percent the products that can be imported from Argentina duty free under the Generalized System of Preferences, a programme designed to help developing countries by eliminating tariffs on some of their exports.

"I have determined that Argentina fails to provide adequate and effective means under its laws for foreign nationals to secure, to exercise and to enforce exclusive rights in intellectual property," Clinton said in the order.
"As a result, I have determined to withdraw benefits for 50 percent (approximately $260 million) of Argentina's exports under the GSP programme," Clinton said in the order.

Dozens of products -- chemicals, certain metals and metal products, a variety of manufactured goods, raw sugar, garlic, fish milk protein concentrate and anchovies -- are to be removed from the programme within 30 days, the U.S. Trade Representative's office said.
"The action taken today will remain in effect until Argentina takes steps to improve its (intellectual property) protection," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in a statement.
She said the action was being taken because Argentina failed to bring its laws protecting patents and other intellectual property into compliance with longstanding commitments.
Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella condemned the move as "an unnecessary and arbitrary blow to such a firm political and trading ally as Argentina."

He said Argentina's new patent laws were perfectly in line with World Trade Organisation rules and added: "Argentina will bear these measures but the government will not modify its legislation which is completely satisfactory."
In the Argentine Congress, the lower house's Industry Committee said it was preparing a bill with retaliatory measures that could include slapping taxes on U.S. cola imports.
The United States has been pressing Argentina for years to strengthen its patent protection laws and complained that measures approved last year did not go far enough.
Until 1995, Argentine law set no restrictions at all on copying foreign drug patents. The U.S. drugs industry says it loses $500 million a year to Argentine patent piracy.
Washington specifically objects to the new laws setting a five-year transition period for patent protection. Argentina argues that it could by right have taken 10 years.
In January the U.S. government issued a notice that it intended to withdraw the GSP preferences.
